text:
Dear Dr. Vance,

Thank you for evaluating this six-month-old infant whom I am referring for multidisciplinary assessment. 

The infant first presented around five months of age with increasing irritability and poor feeding. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an infratentorial mass that underwent urgent neurosurgical decompression. Histopathology of the resected tissue demonstrated a malignant intracranial embryonal neoplasm with sheet-like architecture, abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, and characteristic rhabdoid cytomorphology. 

Subsequent systemic staging revealed an additional large, solitary mass within the right renal parenchyma. A percutaneous core needle biopsy was performed, and tissue examination confirmed a distinct, poorly differentiated primary malignant renal neoplasm showing prominent rhabdoid cellular features. 

The infant was born at 39 weeks following an uncomplicated pregnancy, with normal neonatal screens. General physical examination is otherwise unremarkable; the child is afebrile with normal vital signs, clear lung fields, a regular heart rhythm, and no peripheral lymphadenopathy. The abdomen is soft with a palpable right flank fullness, but no distension. The cranial surgical wound is healing well, and pupils are briskly reactive bilaterally. There is no known family history of pediatric neoplasms, and the parents report no consanguinity. Current medications are limited to maintenance levetiracetam and supportive famotidine.

Given the presentation of these two aggressive malignant lesions, I would greatly appreciate your evaluation and recommendations regarding systemic management and overall treatment strategy.

Sincerely,
Dr. Catherine Hughes
Pediatric Oncology Service
